title: Folio 6: The Sultan and the Lion
description: Sick with fever, his club missed and his spear snapped, a young prince faced a wounded lion with nothing but his hands. Beyhaqi saw Masud of Ghazni hunt lions alone, stand barefoot in the snow, and kill eight lions in a day. But what does a lion hunt tell us about a king who would soon face enemies no spear could stop?
source: Tarikh-e Beyhaqi, volume six: the portrait of Amir Masud's habits and hunting (section on lion hunting: his training, winter hunts, the lion near Kikanan on the road to Multan, the elephant hunt in India, eight lions in one day near Herat, Bu Sahl Zawzani's Arabic verses), read in the Persian text (Ganjoor, Fayyaz edition p. 143); background from Encyclopaedia Iranica and Wikipedia ('Mas'ud I of Ghazni', 'Bahram V')
cold_open: Reed beds near the road to Multan. A young prince, shaking with fever, has thrown his club and missed. His spear is in the lion's chest, and his arms are too weak to hold it. The spear breaks.
paragraphs: Welcome to The Honest Historian. I'm Mehdi Rahmani, and this is Folio Six. Today there are no plots in the palace and no letters in the chancery. Today we go out into the reed beds, where something large is moving in the dark.
A prince with a fever. A spear in his hand. And a lion that does not fall. This is a true scene, written down by a man who served that prince for many years.

First, let me remind you who our prince is. His name was Masud. He was the son of Mahmud of Ghazni, the great conqueror, and in the year ten thirty he became sultan himself, after the struggle with his brother that we followed in Folios Two and Three.

When Beyhaqi wrote his history, he did not only list battles and dates. He stopped, here and there, to paint a portrait. And in one part of his book, he sets down what kind of man Masud was in his body and in his habits. He tells us about the sultan's strength, his hunting, and his stubborn love of hardship. Today's story comes from those pages.

Now, a word of warning before we begin. Beyhaqi served Masud for years. He admired him, and he wrote while Masud's own family still ruled. So we will listen to these stories with open ears, but also with a careful mind. Keep that in your pocket. We will come back to it.

Beyhaqi begins with the young Masud. Even as a boy, he says, the prince trained his body hard. He tested his strength. He lifted heavy stones. He wrestled. He liked to set traps for waterbirds and other birds, and he had places built for catching them.

Then Beyhaqi adds something he saw with his own eyes. On days of bitter cold and heavy snow, Masud would ride out to hunt. He would get down from his horse in the snow and stay out in the freezing air for hours, from one prayer time almost to the next. Sometimes, in that cold, he pulled on his boots with nothing on his feet.
Why would a prince do this? Beyhaqi tells us Masud's own reason. A man must get used to hardship, he said, so that when a real crisis comes, he is not helpless.
In Persian, the line is short and plain.
Bar chenin chizha khuy bayad kard.
One must get used to such things.
I like that sentence. It is the voice of a soldier, not a poet. Hold on to it, because the rest of this story is about a man who trained himself for every kind of danger. Or at least, for one kind.
Then Beyhaqi turns to lions.

In those days there were lions in Iran, and in the lands that are now Afghanistan and Pakistan. They lived in the thickets and reed beds along the rivers. Today they are gone from all of those places. But in Masud's time, a lion hunt was the greatest test a nobleman could face.

Most princes hunted lions the safe way. Their servants and soldiers did the dangerous work, and the prince took the glory. Masud, Beyhaqi tells us, did not. He hunted lions alone, and he would not let his servants help him. Beyhaqi lists the places where he did it, across the eastern lands, from the region of Herat in the west down toward Bust and Ghazni.

He also tells us exactly how Masud did it. The prince carried two weapons. One was a short, heavy throwing weapon, something like a club or a short javelin. The other was a short, thick spear. First he threw the club. If that did not stop the lion, he planted his spear and took the lion's charge on its point, and held it there while the animal twisted and fought, until it grew weak and fell. Only with the fiercest lions did he let his men come in with swords and axes.
It is a terrifying method. Everything depends on the strength of one man's arms, at the moment when a lion is throwing its whole weight against him.
Now comes the scene I promised you.

It happened before Masud was sultan. Beyhaqi tells us that, for a time, his father Mahmud was displeased with him, and the young prince was sent away toward Multan, in what is now Pakistan. Why was Mahmud angry? Beyhaqi says only that it is a long story, and he does not tell it here. So neither will I.

On that journey, near a place called Kikanan, Masud met a lion. And he was ill. He had what was called a quartan fever, a fever that comes back again and again, every few days, and leaves a man weak and shaking.
He did not turn back. He went at the lion in his usual way.
He threw his club. But the lion ducked, and the club flew over its head.

So he took the charge on his spear, as he had done so many times before. The spear went into the lion's chest. But this time the fever had taken his strength. He could not hold it. The lion broke the spear and came straight at him.
Stop for a moment and picture it. A sick young man, alone, his club gone, his spear in pieces, and a wounded lion on top of him.
What did he do?

Beyhaqi tells us that Masud struck the lion with his bare hands, both hands, on the head and the face. The lion went down. Masud held it down, and shouted for his men. One of his guards ran in and finished the animal with a sword.
Everyone who saw it was astonished. And Beyhaqi says they agreed on one thing. The old story of Bahram Gur, the story they had all read in books, must be true after all.

Who was Bahram Gur? He was a king of ancient Persia, of the Sasanian family, who lived some six hundred years before Masud. In Persian poetry and legend, he is the great hunter king. The most famous tale says that, to win his throne, he took the royal crown from between two hungry lions.
So the men around Masud were saying something quite bold. We always thought those stories were exaggerated. Now we have seen it with our own eyes. Our prince is a new Bahram.
Beyhaqi has two more lion stories for us.

The second happened later, in India. This time Masud was hunting from the back of an elephant. As was the custom, the elephant's head was covered with iron. Suddenly a big lion burst out of the thicket and attacked the elephant.

Masud threw his club, and wounded the lion in the chest. But the lion was not finished. It leapt onto the elephant from behind. The great animal was shaking under him. Masud went down on one knee, on the elephant's back, and struck once with his sword. Beyhaqi says that single blow cut off both of the lion's front legs. The lion fell and died. Those who were there said they had never heard of anything like it.

The third story is about numbers. Before he took the throne, Masud went out on a day's hunt on the way toward Herat. That day, Beyhaqi tells us, he killed eight lions, and caught a ninth alive with a lasso.
And here, our narrator steps into his own story.

That evening, back at the tent, there was wine, and everyone talked about the lions and praised the prince. A courtier asked for paper and ink, and on the spot he wrote a poem in Arabic in Masud's honor. The courtier was Bu Sahl Zawzani. If you heard Folio Five, you know that name. He was the clever, bitter rival of Beyhaqi's teacher.

Masud liked the poem, and it was copied out. Beyhaqi tells us that he was standing right there, and that he copied it too. But then, he says, he lost his copy over the years. So in his book he writes down only the lines he still remembers, and he tells us so.
That small confession is pure Beyhaqi. He could have filled the page and nobody would have known. Instead he tells us, plainly, this is from memory, and some of it is gone.

Then he adds a comment. There was an old Arabic saying about poets. The best poetry is the most false. In other words, the most beautiful praise is usually a lie. But not here, says Beyhaqi. The prince really did have all these qualities, and more. The poet did not need to exaggerate.
So now, let us take that careful mind out of our pocket.

Is Beyhaqi flattering his old master here? Perhaps a little. He loved Masud, he served him, and he wrote under Masud's family. But notice what he does. He tells us where these things happened. He tells us which things he saw himself. He admits what he forgot. And he leaves out the story of Mahmud's anger rather than tell it badly. That is not how a flatterer writes. That is how a witness writes, even a fond one.

And here is the deeper point. Beyhaqi does not only show us Masud the lion killer. In other parts of the same book, as we heard in Folio Five, he shows us a sultan who did not always listen to good advice. A sultan who could be stubborn, proud and sure of himself.

Put those two pictures side by side, and you see the whole man. Masud trained his body for every hardship. He would face a lion alone, sick, with his bare hands. But a lion is a single enemy, in a single moment, and courage alone can beat it. The dangers that were coming for Masud were different. Slow, patient horsemen from the steppe. Quarrels among his own generals. Hard choices that needed listening, not strength.

Bar chenin chizha khuy bayad kard. One must get used to such things. Masud got used to snow and fever and lions. Whether he ever got used to hearing a hard truth is a question Beyhaqi lets us answer for ourselves.
If there is one lesson here, it is this: courage wins the fight in front of you, but only wisdom sees the fight that is coming.

Next week, we meet one of the old guard of the empire. Altuntash, the governor of Khwarazm, a general loyal to Mahmud, suspected by Masud, and the hero of a story about loyalty that ends at a deathbed.

If you enjoyed this story, follow the show so you don't miss the next one, and share it with someone who loves history. I'm Mehdi Rahmani. This episode was retold from the Persian original of the History of Beyhaqi, and narrated with an AI rendering of my own voice. Thank you for listening.
